newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan says Iraq must stop threatening neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Jordan says Iraq must stop threatening neighbours.

text.p: Jordan said on Monday Iraq had to change its aggressive posturing against its neighbours if it wanted to regain the trust of the international community.

"There is hope that Iraq's political language will rise to a level where its neighbours don't feel under any threat," Information Minister Marwan Muasher told a news conference. "We don't feel that has happened until now."
Muasher did not specify which of Iraq's neighbours -- Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Syria, Turkey or Iran -- he was referring to.
Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti said on Sunday Jordan wanted Iraq to "take steps, legal and political, to reassure world public opinion" about its intentions.
Jordan refused to join a U.S.-led military coalition which expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991, it has since distanced itself from Iraqi President Saddam Hussein.
King Hussein publicly called for change in Baghdad last year, giving refuge to two high-profile Iraqi defectors and allowing Iraqi opposition groups to set up offices in Amman.

But Jordan has tried to play down the poor political ties in the search for business opportunities with its biggest trading partner ahead of the imminent implementation of the $2 billion Iraq-U.N. oil-for-food deal which would allow Iraqi oil exports for the first time since it invaded Kuwait in 1990.
Kabariti met Iraqi Trade Minister Mohammed Mehdi Saleh on Monday to discuss supplying Baghdad with food and medicine under the U.N. deal.

Jordanian vegetable oil, pharmaceutical and detergent producers are eager to increase their sales to Baghdad, and Jordan hopes that increased use of its only port, at Aqaba on the Red Sea, will also breath life into its economy.

"We welcome the participation of Jordanian companies and traders to export commodities and food," Saleh said after the talks. "We have discussed how to enlarge our use of Aqaba in importing our commodities through the (oil-for-food deal) as well as our trade for different commodities," he said.
